topic.subject: science
topic.title: Combustion and flame
topic.scope: combustible substances, ignition temperature, fire extinguishers, types of combustion, zones of a flame, fuel efficiency

misconceptions.statement: Combustion is a physical change because the fuel just disappears.
misconceptions.why: Students observe the fuel vanishing and don't see the gaseous products formed.
misconceptions.fix: Combustion is a chemical change where fuel reacts with oxygen to form new substances like CO2 and water vapor.

probe.question: If you burn 1kg of wood, why does the remaining ash weigh much less?
probe.wrong_answer: Because the matter was destroyed or turned into nothing.

misconceptions.root_belief: what you cannot see does not exist
misconceptions.source_hint: HBCSE diagnostic research on chemical changes

misconceptions.statement: A substance with a high ignition temperature catches fire very easily.
misconceptions.why: Students confuse 'high' with 'high reactivity' or 'high speed'.
misconceptions.fix: Ignition temperature is the minimum temperature required; a lower ignition temperature means it catches fire more easily.

probe.question: Substance A has an ignition temperature of 40°C and B has 400°C. Which is more dangerous to store?
probe.wrong_answer: Substance B because it has a higher temperature.

misconceptions.root_belief: bigger or more means more effect

misconceptions.statement: Air is the fuel that burns in a fire.
misconceptions.why: Students see that blowing on a fire makes it grow, assuming air is the source of the fire.
misconceptions.fix: Air (oxygen) is only a supporter of combustion; the substance being consumed (like wood or wax) is the fuel.

probe.question: In a candle flame, what is actually being used up as the primary source of energy?

misconceptions.root_belief: the agent of change is the source

misconceptions.statement: Water is the best way to put out an electrical fire.
misconceptions.why: Generalization that water puts out all fires from everyday experience with wood fires.
misconceptions.fix: Water conducts electricity and can give the person a shock; use CO2 or sand for electrical fires.

probe.question: Why shouldn't we use water on a fire caused by a short circuit?
probe.wrong_answer: Because water will make the fire spread faster like oil.

misconceptions.root_belief: a rule for one case works everywhere

misconceptions.statement: The yellow part of a candle flame is the hottest zone.
misconceptions.why: Yellow and orange are intuitively associated with heat (like the sun or glowing iron).
misconceptions.fix: The outermost blue zone is the hottest because it has a continuous supply of oxygen for complete combustion.

probe.question: Which part of the flame should a goldsmith use to melt gold?

misconceptions.root_belief: brightest or most colorful is most intense

misconceptions.statement: Spontaneous combustion happens without any reason or heat.
misconceptions.why: The lack of an visible external spark makes it seem like magic or 'no cause'.
misconceptions.fix: It happens when a substance reaches its ignition temperature due to internal heating (like bacterial action or oxidation).

probe.question: How can a heap of hay catch fire on its own in a barn?
probe.wrong_answer: It just happens randomly without any temperature change.

misconceptions.root_belief: events without visible causes have no cause

misconceptions.statement: A fuel with a higher calorific value is always the 'best' fuel.
misconceptions.why: Focusing on energy output while ignoring safety, cost, and pollution.
misconceptions.fix: An ideal fuel must have high calorific value AND be cheap, easy to store, and non-polluting.

probe.question: Is Hydrogen the best domestic fuel because it has the highest calorific value?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because it gives the most heat.

misconceptions.root_belief: more of one good attribute makes the whole best

misconceptions.statement: Fire is a form of matter, like a gas.
misconceptions.why: Fire occupies space and moves, leading students to categorize it as a substance.
misconceptions.fix: Fire is a process (a chemical reaction) and the flame is the region where gases glow; it is not a substance itself.

probe.question: If you put fire in a sealed jar, does the weight of the jar increase because of the fire?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because fire is a gas and gas has weight.

misconceptions.source_hint: Rosalind Driver's research on the nature of fire

misconceptions.statement: Incomplete combustion only produces smoke, not any dangerous gases.
misconceptions.why: Smoke is visible, while Carbon Monoxide is invisible and its danger is not immediately apparent.
misconceptions.fix: Incomplete combustion produces Carbon Monoxide, a highly poisonous gas that can be fatal in closed rooms.

probe.question: Why is it dangerous to sleep in a closed room with a coal fire?
probe.wrong_answer: Because the smoke will make you cough and wake up.

misconceptions.root_belief: what you cannot see cannot hurt you

misconceptions.statement: Metals are non-combustible and can never burn.
misconceptions.why: In daily life, metal utensils are used over fire without burning.
misconceptions.fix: Many metals like Magnesium or Sodium are highly combustible under the right conditions.

probe.question: What happens when a magnesium ribbon is heated over a burner?
probe.wrong_answer: It just melts because metals don't burn.

misconceptions.root_belief: everyday experience applies to all conditions

misconceptions.statement: Blowing on a candle puts it out because you are removing the oxygen.
misconceptions.why: Students know fire needs oxygen and think their breath 'pushes' it away.
misconceptions.fix: Blowing puts out a candle primarily by cooling the vapors below their ignition temperature.

probe.question: Why does a small candle go out when you blow on it, but a bonfire gets bigger?
probe.wrong_answer: Because your breath has no oxygen for the candle but has oxygen for the bonfire.

misconceptions.root_belief: one action has only one possible mechanism

misconceptions.statement: The wick of the candle is what burns to produce the flame.
misconceptions.why: The wick is where the flame is attached and it turns black/disappears.
misconceptions.fix: The wax vapors are the actual fuel; the wick just helps transport the liquid wax upwards.

probe.question: If you could remove the wax but keep the wick, would the candle burn for hours?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because the wick is the fuel.

misconceptions.root_belief: the most central part is the source
misconceptions.source_hint: Faraday's Chemical History of a Candle (educational adaptations)
